2474.prule: Two lexical tonemes, high (marked, 44) vs low (unmarked, 22), contrasting on monosyllables and disyllables; in disyllabic words the tonal contrast is realised only on the second syllable, the first carrying a default mid/level pitch, which the authors attribute to 'the stress is always on the second syllable' in disyllables. 2474.tone: All first-hand descriptions reached (Jacquesson 2003; Subbarao et al. 2010; Hoque 2014, 2016; S. Debbarma 2014; Veikho & Mushahary 2015; Sh. Debbarma 2021; Joseph & Burling 2001: 52; Dhar 1983) treat Kokborok as a two-tone language, high vs low (Sh. Debbarma 2021: three, after Debnath 2014). Veikho & Mushahary 2015 measure F0 on 5 speakers of the Debbarma (standard) variety: two tonemes, low unmarked, high marked; the disyllabic minimal pairs (25)-(31) are all 22-22 vs 22-44, so the contrast sits on the final syllable. The only placement statement about stress is the unmeasured explanatory aside in the conclusion, 'in disyllabic words, the stress is always on the second syllable' (first syllable default mid/level tone) (disyllables final, quantity-insensitive; nothing for longer words). Chakraborty 1981: 15-16 says Tipra has both tone (svar) and stress (jhõk); p. 16, translated: 'I have already mentioned that the Tipra language has jhõk. This jhõk is not like the stress of English or Bengali.... In the speech flow of Tipra, stress falls in two ways. One, in particular words: for instance, if for "egg" the word butui is used instead of taktui or takhumtui, then to keep it apart from the nearly homophonous butui meaning "broth", a jhõk at the beginning of butui "egg" becomes obligatory. Two, if the final vowel of a group is a tense-marking verb suffix, a case ending or a particle, then a jhõk falls on that final vowel.'

2476.dq: Lexical items each have their own (in Kombai unpredictable) main word stress but functors tend to be unstressed. [p.89]

2476.prule: Main word stress is lexically contrastive (phonemic) and explicitly 'unpredictable': disyllables contrast initial vs final stress (xúⁿdo 'meat' vs xuⁿdó 'foot'; réᵑge 'red' vs reᵑgé 'penis'). Each lexical item carries its own main word stress; functors (relators, cliticised postpositions) tend to be unstressed; in modifier-head compound nouns the first (modifying) stem takes the main word stress. No default position, no weight condition.

The primary description calls it stress and phonemic/unpredictable, so the record is coded lexical; tone or pitch accent is a defensible alternative label a reviewer may prefer.

2479.tone: Sec. 2.6.2 (p. 28): 'There is phonemic word tone. On one, two and three syllable words, the contrastive patterns are a fall-rise, a rising, a rise-fall, a falling and a fall-fall tone pattern over the word. The fall-rise is by far the most common.' The author adds that the contrast may reduce to rising vs falling on the last syllable, that 'Unlike stress, tone does not change when the word is pronounced in isolation', and that stress (amplitude) and tone graphs 'usually follow each other' but diverge in some words, with 'no significance' found. So Konai is a word-tone language with an explicit, separate, predictable final-stress statement; sec. 2.6 intro (p. 27): 'Stress and length are predictable; nasalisation and tone are not.'

2485.dq: The syllable is the unit of stress in Korku. ... A set of rules which characterises every syllable of every Korku PW [phonological word] as either "stressed" or "unstressed" on the basis of this position and strength data is discussed at length in this chapter. (Zide 1979: 161 and fn. 2; Zide 2008: 260 leaves intonation as 'a subject for future research')
2485.dloc: Zide 1979: 161-162 (definition, phonemic-stress residue), 165 fn. 1 (strength-level formulae: CV́C vs CV́), 168 fn. 9 (short syllables as 4°), 169-170 (strength table, Rules I-IV, amendments, examples (1)-(4)); Zide 2008: 260 (sec. 2.5 'Intonation/stress', Google Books).
2485.heavy: Closed syllables are heavy: 'closed syllables, those with final consonant, are heavier than open syllables' (Zide 2008: 260). Zide 1979: 169 gives a five-degree strength scale read off consonant-vowel-semivowel shape (p. 169 strength table): 1° CV́C, C̄VC, VC̄, CVC, CV^C (formulae Ś,s,s,S,S); 2° CVC, CV́, VC (S,ź,x); 3° CV, #V (post-open juncture V), a (Z,Z,A); 4° WV, ^ccV, C̄V, C^V (Y,z,z,v); 5° V(≠a) (z). The acute over V marks phonemic stress (p. 162: 'Phonemic stress is indicated by |'| over the syllable vowel'); the tick over a C in C̄VC, VC̄ and C̄V is Zide's ambisyllabic-consonant bar (p. 163: 'the symbol C̄ can be defined as Xi(C2)/Xj(C1), i.e. it is ambisyllabic'p. 165 fn. 1: 'Note that C̄VC (unlike C̄V) is distinguishable from the other syllables on its strength level'), and the superscript C/cc marks the same ambisyllabic consonant as coda or onset; the fourth 1° entry CVC shows no mark on. No entry is a tone or accompaniment class: p. 162 '"A" have no effect on stress weights and will not be mentioned further in this connection' (the accompaniments being nasalisation and the two aspiration-low-tone phonemes). Vowel length is not phonemic; 'short syllables' (short-vowel nuclei) count as 4° (p. 168 fn. 9: '<3-4-3-3-3> <+---+> where the 4 is a short syllable'). Onsetless and semivowel-onset syllables are weaker than CV, so the scale also reads off onsets.
2485.dflt: Final syllable stressed (Rule I) and initial syllable stressed, with further stresses counted rightward from the initial: Rule III marks the first syllable of the initial unmarked stretch and every odd-numbered syllable following it until no supra-minimal unmarked stretch remains (a medial stretch of two syllables is minimal); Rule IV stresses the initial syllable of a PW that would otherwise have only its final stress. All-open 3° (CV) words: /gada/ CVCV 3-3 -> <++.> (p. 170); /tipikiba/ <Z-Z-Z-Z> -> <+--+> (p. 167); <3-3-3-3-3> -> <+-+-+> (p. 168 fn. 9).
2485.prule: Weight- and position-driven multiple stress: every syllable of a phonological word (PW) is marked + or -. The final syllable is always stressed (Rule I; the penult instead when the final is a 'lengthening' or 'diphthongisation'); every 1° syllable (the strongest closed-syllable types: phonemically stressed CV́C, C̄VC and VC̄ with an ambisyllabic consonant, CVC, CV^C) is stressed; every 2° syllable (CVC, CV́, VC) is stressed when bordered by a weaker syllable or by preceding open juncture, so a word-initial closed syllable is always stressed; any open 3°/4° syllable preceding a still weaker one is stressed (Rule II); remaining unmarked stretches are broken by alternating stress (Rule III); a word left with a single (final) stress also stresses its initial syllable (Rule IV, so /gada/ 'river' is <++>). Zide 2008: 260 summarises: 'Stress is largely automatic, determined by the syllable weight (closed syllables, those with final consonant, are heavier than open syllables) and position, final position syllables having more weight than initial ones.'
2485.srule: The source ranks no stress above another: every syllable is simply stressed (+) or unstressed (-), and words routinely carry several stresses. With the always-stressed final syllable (Rule I) taken as the main stress, the other stresses fall: (Rule II) on every 1° (strongest, closed or phonemically stressed) syllable, on every 2° syllable (CVC, VC, CV́) bordered by a weaker syllable or by preceding open juncture (so a word-initial closed syllable is always stressed), and on any 3°/4° open syllable preceding a weaker one; (Rule III) by binary alternation across each remaining unstressed stretch (the first syllable of a word-initial stretch and every odd-numbered syllable after it; the second syllable of a homogeneous medial stretch); (Rule IV) on the initial syllable of a word that would otherwise carry only the final stress. Examples: /kokosomoroden/ <+-+-++>, /mudakekukiba/ <-+-+-+>, /kokoyoba/ <+--+>, /gada/ <++>; an all-light five-syllable word <+-+-+> (p. 168 fn. 9).

2490.tone: Heeschen 1978 (Irian 7(2): 12-13, read from an image-only scan) reports second-hand that 'tones are said to be phonemic in Nalca and Kosarek (Bromley 1973:15 and Rule and Cutting)', adds 'Though I have not found any minimal pair in Nalca and Kosarek', and derives the tonal features from syllable contraction and word-final glottal stop, concluding that 'tonal features develop only in certain restricted environments' and that 'the tonal analysis of Nalca and Kosarek may be partly right, though... tones have to be marked only on a very limited set of the vocabulary'. 2491.prule: Stress is mobile and non-automatic; it falls on the 1st or the 2nd syllable of the word, with no rule stated for which (Kodzasov, p. 339; general p. 318: word stress in Daghestanian languages is 'always mobile and non-automatic'). In noun inflection (note 117) any oblique-stem suffix may bear stress: monosyllabic roots always shift stress to the suffix; disyllabic roots either keep it on the root (mizmíz - mizmíz-i) or shift it to the suffix with syncope of the medial root vowel (mudúr - mudr-í), lexically. When inflection would put stress on the 3rd syllable, the pretonic vowel is dropped (ʕaršíl - ʕaršlár), keeping stress within the first two syllables.

tn.translation: Ikota is a tone language, a frequent feature of African and Asian languages. It has two levels of melodic pitch: high and low. As for the (consonant and vowel) phonemes, tones will be identified by commutation. The phonological identity of the high tone and the low tone emerges from the following comparisons: èbókà 'song' / èbòkà 'bench', ìkáká 'palm' / ìkàká 'family' ... [fn. 2] Tone refers to a melodic pitch assigned to each vowel. In other words, all vowels in Ikota carry a tone.

2494.prule: Stress always on the penultimate syllable, without exception, schwa (pepet) penults included (Collins 1995: 'tekanan selalu jatuh pada suku kata praakhir tanpa kekecualian; jadi suku kata yang bervokal pepet pun ditekankan juga'). GROUP-LEVEL STATEMENT: Collins states it for the ancestor of 'semua dialek Melayu Borneo' in a diachronic frame (the original stress system 'changed; everything was levelled so that stress always falls on the penult'), listing it as innovation 1 of three (penult stress shift, medial-consonant gemination, penult vowel 'heavying') and adding that Brunei Malay and Bacan show only steps 1 and 3. Kota Bangun is tied to the rule by membership only: it is the Kutai member of the same page's East-Borneo tree; Collins 1994 JDB 38 compares 'dialek Kutai varian Kota Bangun dengan dialek Brunei' using 'pemanjangan konsonan dan pemindahan tekanan' as branch criteria; and Jaludin Chuchu 2003/2008 (restating Collins 1991/1994) frames the same three changes as 'tiga perubahan khusus di antara DMTB dengan dialek Melayu di Kalimantan Timur', with the Kota Bangun dialect as the East Kalimantan dialect under discussion (gemination after a former-schwa penult in disyllabic words: [mannok], [pattan], [pissan]), which Kota Bangun retains. No opened text states the synchronic rule for Kota Bangun in a sentence of its own. Stress is not contrastive (Suryadikara et al. 1979:10: no suprasegmental phonemes in Kutai incl. KKB). Stricter readers who refuse group-level statements would code not determinable from the sources; both checks chose fixed-penult.

2498.dq: Nicolaï 1982:281: "l'accent peut tomber sur la dernière ou l'avant dernière syllabe du 'mot'"; Prost 1956:37: "Dans les mots de deux syllabes, la première est en général à la fois accentuée et allongée" (Prost also notes unaccented monosyllabic function words: "Il y a des monosyllabes inaccentués qui sont des « mots-outils », particules de conjugaison et pospositions").
2498.dloc: Nicolaï 1982: p.281 (§4, 'Type 2'); Prost 1956: p.37, ch. IV 'Accent', §69.
2498.prule: Three first-hand descriptions of the Songhay of Gao disagree and none states a usable word-stress rule. Nicolaï 1982 (typology p.281; derivation §19-20 pp.303-306): 'système accentuel à liberté limitée' -- the accent falls on the final or the penultimate syllable of the word, never on the initial syllable of a trisyllable; the class is lexical (reflex of proto-Songhay tone schemes; RR12: final accent unless a former non-monotone non-high contour stood on P2, then penult); the contrast is weakly perceptible and carried by slight pitch/tension, not intensity; fn.11 leaves open whether the system is accentual or tonal. Prost 1956 p.37 §69: intensity accent generally on the FIRST syllable of disyllables (often with lengthening), sometimes both syllables equally accented; syllables after a CC cluster or after ŋ are very weak. Heath 1999 §3.9 (excerpt grade): no lexical or grammatical tonal (prosodic) distinctions; Nicolaï's minimal pairs could not be confirmed with Nicolaï re-listening (taari 'lie' = taari 'mat'); residual surface pitch differences reflect vowel length; no stress/accent section in the phonology chapter.
2498.srule: Not mentioned in Nicolaï 1982 (§4 p.281, §§19-23 pp.303-308: one word accent, final or penultimate, nothing on secondary or rhythmic accent) or in Prost 1956 (p.37 §§69-71: intensity accent of disyllables and weak post-cluster syllables only); Heath 1999 ch.3 (Google Books) has no stress section.

2499.dq: 1.15 Word Level Stress. Though there are minimal pairs distinguished only by phonemic stress, in the majority of instances word level stress is determined by the morphological structure of the word, the number of syllables, syllabic shape and type of vowel.
2499.dloc: Sec. 1.15 'Word Level Stress', pp. 29-32; quote from p. 29 (1.15, 1.15.2) and p. 31 (1.15.3); monosyllables 1.15.1 p. 29; suffix exceptions p. 32
2499.heavy: Full (non-shwa) vowel vs. shwa/reduced vowel, used only as a subsidiary conditioner: in bisyllables a full vowel takes stress over a shwa (shwa+full -> final; full+reduced -> first), and a noun stem containing shwa cedes stress to the first syllable in trisyllabic nouns (pp. 29, 31). Not a weight-based stress system: the main determinant is the stem.
2499.dflt: Bisyllables with two full vowels: first syllable; with two shwas: first syllable if the word ends in a vowel, final syllable if it ends in a consonant (p. 29).
2499.prule: Primary stress falls on the stem syllable: in verbs the stem is word-final (or penultimate when a suffix follows); in nouns the stem is stressed unless its vowel is schwa, in which case a trisyllabic noun stresses its first syllable; nouns of more than three syllables behave like verbs. Monosyllables are stressed (1.15.1). Bisyllables are decided by word class and vowel quality: verbs, and schwa+full-vowel words, stress the final syllable; full+reduced and full+full words stress the first; schwa+schwa words stress the first if vowel-final and the last if consonant-final. Some minimal pairs are distinguished only by stress.
2499.srule: At most one secondary stress per word: in trisyllabic words with final primary stress it falls on the first syllable; in words of more than three syllables it falls two syllables before the primary-stressed syllable; all other syllables are unstressed.

2499.tone: Kroul 1975 describes the Central Outer (Central) dialect as a stress language and does not mention tone. Jette & Jones 2000 (KAD intro, Krauss's dialect section, read in an earlier compilation) reports low-marked tone retained only in Lower Koyukon and the Toklat-Bearpaw subdialect of Upper Koyukon; Axelrod 1993 p. 11: 'Koyukon shows only vestigial tone, only for some speakers'. So the language of this record has a marginal tonal dialect not covered by Kroul's stress statement.

2499.sec_quote: Secondary stress falls on the first syllable in trisyllabic words when primary stress falls on the final syllable. In greater-than-trisyllabic words, secondary stress falls two syllables before the syllable with primary stress. Secondary stress may occur only once in a word, no matter what its length. All syllables which do not have primary or secondary stress are unstressed.
